newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo firms say lack of credits main obstacle - poll.
newsitem.headline: Yugo firms say lack of credits main obstacle - poll.

text.p: Yugoslav firms see lack of credits and working capital as the main obstacles to speedier revival of production, the Belgrade Economics Institute said in its latest August Market Barometer report.

"Lack of credits has been the dominant obstacle for a long period now, which reflects the firmness of monetary policy and access to money flows," Goran Pitic, economist with the institute, told a news conference on Tuesday.
The institute's report is based on a poll of 300 Yugoslav industry and energy firms.
Lack of access to credits was listed as the main problem by 37.5 percent, shortage of raw materials by 24.6 percent, and low demand by 20.6 percent of the firms.
Internal debts were still very high, but firms said they expected the situation to improve slightly in coming months.
According to the Institute for Market Research, internal debts reached 3.98 billion dinars at the end of July when M1 money supply stood at 4.34 billion dinars.
Despite industrial growth of 2.1 percent in August over July, most firms described the economic climate as bad.
After climbing to 6.6 percent in July, inflation slowed to 2.3 percent in August, and was 99.2 percent year-on-year.
"As many as 68.6 percent believe prices will go up in the last quarter, while only 0.7 percent said they expected them to drop," Pitic said.
Use of capacities improved slightly to 55.2 percent over July's 53 percent, but stocks of raw materials and finished goods were very low.
"The overall position of firms was described as bad by 31.8 percent, while 14.2 percent said it was good. This means that they see business risk as very high," Pitic said.
Despite dwindling optimism, 35.5 percent still saw the situation -- particularly domestic demand -- as improving by the year end, but were less hopeful that exports would pick up.

"Since one of the main tasks of economic policy is to strengthen hard currency reserves, it is worrying that as many as 41 percent of the firms said they are not planning exports in the next three months," Pitic said.
Although exports maintained an upward trend, the trade deficit in the January-August period grew to over one billion dollars, with exports worth $1.1 billion and imports $2.265 billion.

Only 27.2 percent of the firms believe there will be investments from local sources, while less than 10 percent said they expected funds from abroad -- despite the prospect of an end to lingering international sanctions. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
